title: Poland Tops Global Arms Imports as Lithuania Funds a US Base and Europe's Rearmament Bill Comes Due
subhead: Poland's $11.9B in 2025 arms imports leads a post-Cold War high in global procurement, while Lithuania moves to pay for a permanent US base and AeroVironment ships Switchblade 600s — the fiscal and industrial cost of Europe's buildup is now the story.

sections.heading: Poland Is Now the World's Largest Arms Importer
sections.body:
Poland's estimated $11.91 billion in arms imports during 2025 makes Warsaw the world's largest importer, according to an assessment by the Centre for Analysis of the World Arms Trade (CAWAT), reported by Defence Security Asia. Poland sits ahead of India, Australia, Taiwan and the United Kingdom.

The ranking is driven by the Abrams main battle tank and K2 Black Panther programmes, which combine large platform deliveries with heavy engineering, recovery and spares requirements. CAWAT estimates global conventional arms imports at at least $119.5 billion for 2025 — described as a post-Cold War high — with cumulative 2022–2025 imports of about $415 billion and a projected $633 billion market for 2026–2029.

The analysis stresses the distinction between procurement and capability: the projected 52.5% increase in spending signals pressure on supply chains rather than an equivalent rise in combat power, because ammunition, spare parts, training pipelines and maintenance capacity determine how fast equipment converts into usable force.
sections.whyItMatters: The world's arms trade is expanding faster than the industrial base that supports it. For Poland and other fast buyers, the binding constraint is no longer money or political will — it is the ability of factories, depots and trainers to absorb and sustain the equipment.

sections.heading: Lithuania Buys a US Base and Its First Switchblade 600s
sections.body:
Lithuania's military has received its first batch of Switchblade 600 loitering munitions from US manufacturer AeroVironment, the Ministry of National Defense said. Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said the munitions let troops 'quickly and very precisely destroy enemy armored vehicles from a safe distance.' The package includes launch and control equipment, a training simulator and maintenance support.

The Switchblade 600 carries an anti-armor warhead, more than 40 minutes of endurance and a demonstrated standoff range above 60 km, extending beyond 90 km with its Forward Pass datalink relay. Lithuania has bought roughly €2 billion in US weapons over three years — Javelins, JLTVs, Black Hawks, HIMARS and AMRAAM — making it the largest US-arms buyer among the Baltic states. Greece, Romania and Sweden have also ordered Switchblade 600s.

Separately, meta-defense reports that Lithuania is ready to fund a permanent US military base on its territory, even as Germany proceeds with a planned brigade deployment and Lithuania raises its own spending. The offer reflects a Baltic preference for a direct, funded US presence over reliance on allied rotational forces.
sections.whyItMatters: Small frontline states are now writing cheques to keep US forces physically present, while loitering munitions move from niche systems to standard infantry kit. Both trends point the same way: deterrence on NATO's eastern edge is increasingly being paid for by the exposed states themselves.

sections.heading: US Navy Adds Cheaper Guns to Shoot Down Cheap Drones
sections.body:
The US Navy is expanding its Mk 38 Mod 4 30mm gun inventory to give warships a low-cost way to defeat drones without burning through surface-to-air missiles. The latest production tranche adds 22 Mk 88 Mod 4 mounts; cumulative reported Mk 38 Mod 4 orders now stand at 55 mounts, per Army Recognition.

Under the first year of a three-year contract, the Navy committed $61.3 million for 22 stabilized mounts and 23 Mk 48 Mod 2 electro-optical sights, disclosed by MS International on October 1. The agreement has a potential value of about $197 million, with deliveries running into January 2031. The Mod 4 is the first caliber increase for the Mk 38 family in more than three decades and adds airburst capability and Aegis integration.

The driver is the cost-exchange problem exposed in the Red Sea: inexpensive unmanned threats forcing ships to expend limited, far costlier interceptors.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the economics of drone defence made concrete. Navies are rebalancing their inner defensive layer toward guns and airburst rounds so that expensive missiles remain reserved for high-end threats — a quiet admission that the cost curve, not just the technology, decides air defence.

sections.heading: France and Türkiye Reopen a Defence Channel With SAMP/T in the Background
sections.body:
France and Türkiye have signed a defence cooperation roadmap after high-level talks in Paris, per Defence24. The document confirms no SAMP/T deal, Meteor arrangement or technology-transfer package — it sets up a political channel and a framework that makes future contracts easier.

The obvious candidate is SAMP/T NG, the long-range air-defence system developed by France and Italy. Cooperation dates to 2017–2018 but stalled amid disputes over Syria, Libya, Greece, Cyprus and the Eastern Mediterranean. President Emmanuel Macron said in July that technical work with Italy and Türkiye was continuing, and Reuters reported France had softened its earlier opposition to a sale.

For Ankara, the logic is layered air defence under its Steel Dome concept plus a high-end system compatible with NATO. The Russian S-400 purchase did the opposite: it removed Türkiye from the F-35 programme, triggered sanctions and left an awkward system to integrate. Moscow has signalled the S-400s could potentially be transferred to a third, Russia-friendly state — which could, if accepted, ease one obstacle to Ankara's return to the F-35 track.
sections.whyItMatters: Türkiye is trying to re-enter the Western defence ecosystem while keeping its own industrial options open. A France-Türkiye air-defence channel, if it becomes contracts, would mark a real shift in European defence politics — and give Washington a path to resolve the S-400 standoff.

sections.heading: Northrop Pushes Sentinel and B-21 as the Credible-Deterrence Case
sections.body:
Northrop Grumman CEO Kathy Warden said modernising US nuclear capabilities is necessary to keep deterrence credible, citing the Sentinel ICBM and B-21 Raider as the company's contributions. 'Deterrence is only as credible as the capabilities behind it,' Warden said, per Defence Industry Europe.

In September, Northrop and the US Air Force said they had fully assembled a Sentinel missile in its vertical operational orientation — a step toward evaluating it for flight testing in 2027. Sentinel is intended to replace the ground-based leg of the triad, with initial capability planned for the early 2030s; Northrop leads more than 500 partners under an engineering and manufacturing development contract aimed at a system viable through 2075. Warden gave no new development milestones.
sections.whyItMatters: With Sentinel's costs and schedule under scrutiny, the contractor is publicly reframing the programme as the backbone of deterrence rather than a budget line. The 2027 flight test and early-2030s fielding dates are the milestones that will decide whether that argument holds.

sections.heading: NATO's Bergen Group Meets in Poland as Washington Pushes 'NATO 3.0'
sections.body:
US officials and European NATO allies are preparing a meeting in Poland under the 'Bergen Group' format — Poland, Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden and Finland — named after the Norwegian city where the first session was held in June, per BGNES. The talks are led by US Under Secretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby.

The meeting sits inside the 'NATO 3.0' concept, through which Washington is pressing for greater European responsibility for the continent's conventional defence. Poland's defence ministry said talks covered European security, Ukraine and its prospects, NATO 3.0, and the US review of its military presence in Europe, with particular attention to Poland. NATO reported a $139 billion increase in defence spending by European allies and Canada in 2025, following the alliance's July 2026 Ankara summit.
sections.whyItMatters: This is where US force-posture decisions and European spending promises get reconciled. For Poland, hosting the talks confirms its central role on the eastern flank — but also puts it under direct pressure to fund the capabilities Washington expects Europe to supply.

bottomLine: Today's developments share one theme: Europe's rearmament is shifting from announcements to bills. Poland is now the world's largest arms importer, Lithuania is offering to fund a permanent US base and has taken delivery of its first Switchblade 600s, and the US Navy is buying cheaper guns precisely because drone defence has become a cost problem. France and Türkiye reopened a defence channel with SAMP/T in the background, Northrop is making the public case for Sentinel and the B-21, and Washington's Bergen Group convenes in Poland to push 'NATO 3.0.' None of these are battlefield events; they are the procurement, industrial and alliance-finance decisions that will shape what forces actually exist in the early 2030s.
sources: Defence Security Asia (CAWAT arms import ranking), Defence Industry Europe (Switchblade 600 delivery to Lithuania; Northrop Grumman on Sentinel/B-21), meta-defense.fr (Lithuania funding a US base), Army Recognition (US Navy Mk 38 Mod 4 30mm expansion), Defence24 (France-Türkiye defence roadmap, SAMP/T), Shephard Media/Defence Insight (Baykar Akinci exports), BGNES (Bergen Group / NATO 3.0 meeting in Poland)
